title: Wall Street Edges Higher as Investors Eye Deals Amid Bond Turmoil
excerpt: All three major indexes gained ground Wednesday in a partial rebound from a three-day losing streak, though rising Treasury yields and Middle East tensions continue to cloud the outlook.
body:
• All three major U.S. indexes gained ground Wednesday, with the S&P 500 rising 0.46% to 7,666.82 after a three-day losing streak
  • The 10-year Treasury yield has surged over 80 basis points since March to 4.79%, nearing the psychologically significant 5% threshold
  • Investors seized on oversold names in airlines, gold miners and regional banks, while the global bond selloff and U.S.-Iran hostilities kept gains in check
  • ADP reported just 38,000 private-sector job additions in August, below expectations, ahead of Friday's closely watched government employment report

Stocks Stage Partial Recovery

Wall Street advanced on Wednesday, snapping a three-day decline as investors scooped up beaten-down stocks even as the global bond selloff and escalating Middle East tensions lingered in the background.

The S&P 500 gained 35.35 points, or 0.46%, to close at 7,666.82. The Nasdaq Composite rose 120.07 points, or 0.46%, to 26,219.85, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 299.37 points, or 0.56%, to 53,066.25. The small-cap Russell 2000 outperformed its larger-cap peers.

Airlines, gold and silver miners, and regional banks led the day's gains, while software and services stocks — seen as vulnerable to AI disruption — underperformed. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has shed nearly a quarter of its value since late June, ticked higher ahead of Broadcom's earnings after the close.

"The war is continuing longer than anyone hoped, and when it ends, energy will cool and inflation won't be as much of an issue. At the same time, we just had a record earnings season, with wonderful fundamentals being driven by the accelerating adoption of AI."

— Lauren Cassidy, Chief Investment Officer, Founders 100 ETF

Bond Selloff Remains the Central Risk

The rebound came with caveats. The 10-year Treasury yield has climbed more than 80 basis points since March to 4.79%, approaching a 5% level that analysts view as a critical threshold for equities. The last time yields reached 5%, in October 2023, broad stock weakness followed.

A renewed round of U.S. airstrikes on Iranian military targets near the Strait of Hormuz pushed oil prices higher, with Brent crude rising to $95.18 per barrel. Tehran responded by targeting U.S. assets across the region, marking the most significant exchange of fire since July and stoking inflation fears.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish comments at Jackson Hole, along with board member Michael Barr's indication that a September rate hike may be necessary, have fueled expectations that borrowing costs will rise further.

Investors Recalibrate After Earnings Season

With second-quarter earnings season now effectively over — a period marked by blowout results that overshadowed macro headwinds — strategists warned that the focus is shifting to fundamentals that may prove less supportive.

"I do think the market's attention now focuses more on these macro factors because you have less of that buffer from the earnings season because it's in the rear-view mirror."

— Keith Lerner, Chief Investment Officer, Truist Advisory Services

The S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings ratio stood at 19.7, down from 22.2 at the start of 2026 but still above the long-term average of 16. Strategists at BlackRock Investment Institute noted that "sticky inflation, heavy government borrowing and growing private investment needs give little reason for pressure on yields to fade."

What's Next

Markets now look to a packed economic calendar, with international trade data, second-quarter productivity figures and the ISM services PMI on Thursday's agenda. Friday's Bureau of Labor Statistics employment report — expected to show 53,000 to 56,000 new jobs — will provide a more comprehensive view of labor market conditions after the weaker-than-expected ADP data.

Among individual stocks, Dell surged after raising its full-year profit and revenue forecast. Uber Technologies gained after announcing plans to cut 10% of its workforce. Nvidia and other chipmakers also ended higher on continued AI momentum.
